objectives: Students will be able to analyze the structural, social, and cultural determinants contributing to health disparities in South Korea.
Students will be able to evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of digital health technologies (e.g., mobile health, telemedicine, wearables, AI) in improving health equity.
Students will be able to apply policy and ethical frameworks to assess the implications of digital health interventions for underserved and vulnerable populations.
Students will be able to critically examine case studies to identify best practices and barriers in implementing digital health strategies within Korean communities.
Students will be able to integrate social work values and principles to design culturally responsive and socially just digital health interventions aimed at reducing disparities.
Students will be able to reflect on personal and professional values to articulate the role of social workers in shaping equitable digital health futures.
topics: Historical overview of health disparities in South Korea
Social determinants of health and their impact on vulnerable populations
The rise of digital health technologies: mobile health, telemedicine, wearables, and AI
Policy frameworks guiding digital health adoption in South Korea
Ethical issues in digital health: equity, privacy, and accessibility
Digital health applications in rural communities and underserved populations
Case studies: successes and challenges of digital health in South Korea
The role of social work in advancing digital health equity
Integrating digital health into community-based care models
Future directions: innovation, sustainability, and culturally responsive digital health strategies

objectives: Students will develop cultural awareness and understanding of South Korea through direct immersion in its communities, institutions, and social systems.
Students will increase knowledge about the rising trends of depression, anxiety, and suicide in South Korea, and the societal factors contributing to these mental health challenges.
Students will gain insight into the prevalence of substance misuse and co-occurring diseases, and critically examine the gaps in prevention, treatment, and recovery services.
Students will explore the transformative role of technology—including digital health tools, AI, and mobile platforms—in addressing mental health and substance misuse disparities.
Students will critically reflect on the intersections of culture, technology, and health equity, and how lessons learned in South Korea can inform global responses to mental health and addiction.
Students will reflect on their group experience abroad, connecting it to personal and professional values, and identifying ways to integrate these lessons into future practice or research.
topics: The rising prevalence of depression, anxiety, and suicide in South Korea: historical and socio-cultural context
Social stigma, systemic barriers, and inequities in mental health and substance misuse treatment
The role of families, schools, and communities in shaping mental health outcomes
Substance misuse in South Korea: trends, risk factors, and social implications
Comparative perspectives: examining disparities in access to care between South Korea and other OECD countries
Innovative models of prevention, treatment, and recovery support
The transformative role of digital health technologies (e.g., telehealth, mobile apps, AI-based interventions) in addres
Case studies of technology-enabled interventions for vulnerable and underserved populations
Ethical considerations in applying technology to mental health care, including privacy, equity, and accessibility
Policy and programmatic responses to mental health and substance misuse: gaps, opportunities, and future directions
Reflections on cross-cultural perspectives and the implications for professional practice in health and social services
